title: Fed Raises Rates for First Time in Three Years, Defying Trump's Demand for Cuts
excerpt: In a unanimous 12-0 vote, Chairman Kevin Warsh led the Federal Reserve's first rate increase since July 2023, lifting the benchmark to 3.75%-4% to fight inflation running near 4% — and signaling one more hike before year-end.
body:
• The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point to 3.75%-4%, the first hike since July 2023, on a unanimous 12-0 vote.
  • Chairman Kevin Warsh — handpicked by President Donald Trump — led the decision, defying the president's repeated public demands for lower rates.
  • Officials signaled another increase before year-end, with the median 2026 rate outlook rising to 4.1% from 3.8%; no further hikes are projected in 2027.
  • Markets slumped on the news: the Dow fell 631 points and the 10-year Treasury yield closed above 5% for the first time in 19 years.

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point on Wednesday, its first increase in more than three years, as Chairman Kevin Warsh and his colleagues moved to confront inflation that has run near 4% — double the central bank's target — for much of the past five years.

The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to lift the federal funds rate to a range of 3.75% to 4%. The decision landed as a rebuke to President Donald Trump, who handpicked Warsh to lead the central bank after repeatedly pressuring the Fed to cut borrowing costs. Warsh has insisted he is acting independently, and Wednesday's move was the clearest demonstration of that claim yet.

"Inflation is too high and has been for too long," Warsh said after the 12-0 vote, according to the Wall Street Journal. "Our decision comes at a time when the American economy appears to be strengthening."

Why the hike, and why now

At his press conference, Warsh said three things had changed since the Fed's July meeting: the economy strengthened, inflation failed to slow, and geopolitical tensions intensified.

Annual inflation as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index has trended closer to 4% than 2% in recent months, and Warsh noted that too many categories of goods and services were posting annualized price gains above 3% over six- and twelve-month windows. The conflict in the Middle East, which CNN reported has lifted oil prices and inflation expectations since early in the year, added urgency: Brent crude has traded above $105 a barrel, feeding directly into consumer prices.

"Stable prices have been the problem now for more than five and a half years," Warsh said, per Barron's. "So what the committee decided to do today was take an action to ensure a timelier return to our price stability objective."

A resilient labor market gave the Fed room to act on inflation without an immediate fear of pushing unemployment higher — the dual mandate's other half is not currently flashing red.

Markets recoil

Stocks and bonds fell as Warsh spoke. The Dow industrials dropped 631 points, or 1.2%, after the press conference began at 2:30 p.m. ET. The S&P 500 lost 0.4%, while the Nasdaq slipped less than 0.1%, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Bonds sold off hard. Short-dated Treasury yields, the most sensitive to Fed policy, surged: the two-year yield erased an early decline to trade at 4.71%. The benchmark 10-year yield settled at 5.003% — the first close above 5% in 19 years. Longer yields are being pushed up by forces Warsh catalogued at length: economic strength, a surge in capital expenditure, and hyperscalers raising funding to feed the AI data-center buildout, which has intensified the competition for capital.

"The surge in capital expenditures, which I referenced in my remarks, is real, and the so-called hyperscalers are out in the market raising funding, and so the competition for capital is real," Warsh said, according to Reuters.

A standoff with the White House

The unanimous vote was the story's political core. Trump installed Warsh expecting an ally for lower rates; instead, Warsh has become the face of renewed tightening. The chairman has repeatedly told reporters that inflation, not presidential preference, drives his decisions.

The new economic projections carry the tension forward: officials' median outlook for rates at the end of 2026 rose to 4.1% from 3.8%, and 16 of 18 policymakers anticipate at least one more quarter-point hike by year's end. But they also project no further increases in 2027 — a sign, as Wells Fargo's Brian Rehling put it, that officials view this as "a targeted adjustment to the current inflation shock rather than the start of a longer tightening cycle."

"We removed a dose of accommodation so that financial and credit conditions would be more consistent with our ultimate objectives."

— Kevin Warsh, Federal Reserve Chairman

Warsh himself submitted no projections, continuing his refusal to offer forward guidance on the future path of rates — a break with Fed tradition that has left markets reading every press conference for clues.

What it means for global money

The hike ripples well beyond US borders. Higher American rates have already lifted the dollar to a seven-week high, pressuring emerging-market currencies including the rupee and raising the cost of dollar-denominated debt. Reuters' Morning Bid noted the move "lifts the hawkish bar" for the Bank of England, which meets Thursday and faces the same energy-driven inflation arithmetic.

For investors, the message is a repricing of the era of cheap money: with US government debt topping $40 trillion and long yields refusing to fall, the world's most important borrowing cost is being set with an inflation fighter's hand.

What to watch next

Attention turns to the December meeting, where the projected second hike of this cycle could land. Incoming inflation prints and any escalation or de-escalation in the Middle East will decide whether Warsh's "measured" two-hike path holds — or whether the Fed, five years into an inflation problem it still hasn't solved, has to do more.
